stances.claim: The new CPRA (April 11, 2023) updated and replaced the 1988 Code in recognition that 'the role of modern-day lawyers has expanded and shifted from advocates to peacemakers, from solicitors to specialists, and from counterparts to collaborators' -- and considered rapid technological advancements shaping lawyer interactions with society, profession, courts, and clients.

The CPRA and the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027 (SPJI) are unequivocal endorsements of CJ's own philosophy of 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law' -- a hi-tech turn that originated in the judiciary and has now been expanded by the Court to cover all attorneys-at-law.
stances.confidence: asserted with humility marker ('I humbly view')

stances.claim: 'Attorney-at-law' refers only to bar-exam passers -- encompassing justices, judges, prosecutors, practicing attorneys, notaries public, and lawyers in government, business, academe, or any capacity requiring bar passage; all are bound by the CPRA oath taken before the Court en banc at the PICC to 'conscientiously and courageously work for justice, as well as safeguard the rights and meaningful freedoms of all persons, identities and communities.'

Sections 36-44 of Canon II (Propriety) detail responsible social-media duties: lawyers must understand benefits, risks, and ethical implications; their posts in any audience-bearing setting must uphold the dignity of the legal profession and shield it from disrepute.
stances.rhetorical_move: verbatim-canon-citation framing for the social-media regime

stances.claim: Four prohibited online acts: (1) knowingly/maliciously posting/sharing/uploading false or unverified disinformation; (2) creating/maintaining hidden-identity accounts to circumvent law or CPRA; (3) revealing confidential client information; and (4) communicating with court/tribunal officers via social media to influence their official performance.

The 15-member sub-committee that finalized the CPRA -- chaired by J Lazaro-Javier with Vice-Chairs Gaerlan and Singh, and 12 members from the CA, SBN, LEB, RTCs of QC and Manila, MeTC of Makati, National Bar Discipline, IBP QC, PALS, PBA, USC, and the OCJ -- deserves acknowledgment for backbreaking spadework.

notable_anecdotes: The role-shift verbatim from the CPRA preamble -- 'from advocates to peacemakers, from solicitors to specialists, and from counterparts to collaborators' -- capturing the new conception of the modern lawyer in three triadic transformations.
Canon VI's 53 sections constituting over a third of the 56-page CPRA -- used to dramatize how heavily the new Code weights accountability and disciplinary process.

CJ's 'unequivocal endorsements of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law' -- a rare moment of CJ explicitly claiming institutional vindication of his own jurisprudential creed.

The CPRA oath verbatim -- 'conscientiously and courageously work for justice, as well as safeguard the rights and meaningful freedoms of all persons, identities and communities' -- taken before the Court en banc at the PICC, the canonical Philippine bar-induction ceremony.
The 'super lawyers of the AI age' coinage -- CJ's fingertip-feel for the rhetorical labeling of the new generation.

The four-prohibited-online-acts catalog -- disinformation, hidden-identity accounts, confidential-info disclosure, and improper officer communications -- laid out as the operative social-media prohibition regime.

The full 15-member sub-committee roster -- with each member's institutional affiliation -- the most extensive personal-acknowledgment paragraph in CJ's recent CPRA columns, modeling backbreaking-spadework appreciation.

one_paragraph_summary: Following his column on the sad saga of Dr. Iggy Agbayani (Nov 13, 2023), which evoked calls to discipline his lawyer, Panganiban begins a two-part series on the new Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA) approved by the SC on April 11, 2023 to replace the 1988 Code of Professional Responsibility. Studying the CPRA, he notes, also means looking at the Court's Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027 (SPJI) unveiled a year ago and detailed in his Sept 25 column -- both turning the judiciary toward hi-tech and AI. The historic turn was expanded by the Court to cover all attorneys-at-law: the old 1988 Code 'reflected the then prevailing trends,' but 'the role of modern-day lawyers has expanded and shifted from advocates to peacemakers, from solicitors to specialists, and from counterparts to collaborators.' The 56-page CPRA is divided into six major Canons, with Canon VI alone containing 53 sections -- over a third of the document -- on the causes and processes by which attorneys are to be held accountable. CJ humbly views the SPJI and CPRA as 'unequivocal endorsements of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law.' He clarifies that 'attorney-at-law' refers only to bar passers -- including justices, judges, prosecutors, practicing attorneys, notaries public, and lawyers in government, business, academe, or any capacity requiring bar passage -- all bound by the CPRA oath taken before the Court en banc at the Philippine International Convention Center to 'conscientiously and courageously work for justice, as well as safeguard the rights and meaningful freedoms of all persons, identities and communities.' Sections 36-44 of Canon II (Propriety) cover responsible social-media use, beginning with the overarching duty to understand the benefits, risks, and ethical implications of social media and to ensure that posts in any audience-bearing public or restricted setting uphold the dignity of the legal profession. The four prohibited online acts: knowingly or maliciously posting/sharing/uploading false or unverified disinformation; operating hidden-identity accounts to circumvent the law or CPRA; revealing confidential client information; and communicating with court/tribunal/agency officers via social media to influence their official duties. He closes by acknowledging the 15-member sub-committee that finalized the CPRA -- chaired by J Amy C. Lazaro-Javier with vice-chairs Samuel H. Gaerlan and Maria Filomena D. Singh, and 12 members from the CA, SBN, LEB, RTCs, MeTC Makati, the National Bar Discipline office, IBP QC, PALS, PBA, USC, and the OCJ. Next Monday: the duties of lawyers to the country and to their clients, like Doctor Agbayani.
